analysis.one_liner: Requires online platforms to implement government-designated copyright-filtering technology or face lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by senators from both parties and pushed by major copyright industries, was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Librarian of Congress designate government-approved technologies that identify, filter, or protect copyrighted works, and would require online service providers to use commercially reasonable efforts to accommodate them. Copyright owners could sue providers that fail to comply and collect statutory damages of $200 to $25,000 per violation, up to $800,000 in the aggregate for repeat violations. The bill also sets up a petition-and-rulemaking process, run by the Copyright Office, through which copyright owners, platforms, and other stakeholders could propose new mandatory measures every three years.
analysis.who_benefits: Large copyright owners — movie studios, music labels, publishers, and other rights holders — gain a new enforcement tool that shifts the cost and labor of policing infringement from themselves to internet platforms. Instead of sending takedown notices one at a time, they could petition the government to designate an identification or filtering technology as mandatory, then sue non-compliant platforms for statutory damages. Technology vendors whose filtering or identification tools get designated also stand to gain, since the bill allows designated measures to be licensed on a "reasonable royalty" rather than purely royalty-free basis.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Studios, labels, and other large copyright owners

how_it_helps.text: Creates a process under which copyright owners can petition the Librarian of Congress to designate technical measures — technologies that identify, protect, or manage copyrighted works — as mandatory, with rulemakings accepted annually within a year of enactment and every three years thereafter.

Gives copyright owners a direct lawsuit against any covered service provider that fails to make reasonable accommodations for a designated measure, with court authority to issue injunctions, award costs and attorney fees, and grant statutory damages of $200–$25,000 per violation — rising to $5,000–$400,000 per violation (capped at $800,000) for providers with a prior violation within three years, and potentially triple damages for three or more violations in five years.
Clarifies that the platform safe harbors of existing copyright law do not shield a provider from this new liability, so the new damages route stands on top of the current system.

Provides some guardrails: the rulemaking must weigh costs, cybersecurity, privacy, effects on competition, fair-use-type interests like criticism and teaching, and possible exemptions for libraries, schools, and small comment-permitting sites; providers can appeal designations to the D.C. Circuit.

analysis.who_pays: Online service providers bear the compliance cost of implementing designated filtering or identification measures, plus litigation risk and statutory damages if a court finds they did not try hard enough — with the smallest platforms and startups least able to absorb either. Their users ultimately pay in restricted services: automated filters are error-prone and can block lawful speech such as commentary, parody, and criticism, and the bill's own rulemaking factors acknowledge risks to privacy, cybersecurity, and fair use. Taxpayers fund the Copyright Office's new advisors and rulemaking process, authorized at $900,000 for fiscal 2023 and $700,000 plus inflation adjustments each year after.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online platforms, their users, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Mandatory filtering technologies can suppress lawful speech. The bill itself requires the Register to weigh the impact on criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research before any designation — an acknowledgment that automated identification tools flag legal content, and history with voluntary filtering systems shows frequent false positives.

Designated measures may be privately owned and licensed on a royalty basis rather than royalty-free, meaning a company holding a patented or proprietary identification technology could have it made mandatory for competitors and platforms — converting its product into a required, paid-for channel.

The statute explicitly requires examination of whether a measure poses an undue cybersecurity threat or creates vulnerabilities, and its impact on privacy and data protection — mandated content surveillance raises real security and privacy concerns.

The damage tiers could be existential for small providers: a startup hosting user comments or uploads that loses one case could face $800,000 in statutory damages for a repeat violation within three years, a sum small sites cannot contest in federal court even with a meritorious defense.

For creators, the good-faith case in favor is real: online piracy costs rights holders income, and the current notice-and-takedown system makes individual creators chase infringement site by site. A designation system is one attempt — though a filtering-first one — to move enforcement upstream.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the large rights holders it serves, the bill is a genuine upgrade: it moves enforcement from manual takedowns to mandatory technology and adds real money damages behind it. But the costs are broadly spread and hard to see — filtering errors that mute lawful speech, compliance burdens that fall hardest on small platforms, a new government process where the industries with the most lobbying muscle file the petitions, and taxpayer-funded administration. The bill includes real safeguards (cost tests, possible exemptions, D.C. Circuit review), yet the core mechanism still locks in industry-designed filtering as the default way copyrighted works are policed online.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC), joined by Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT), introduced the SMART Copyright Act on March 17, 2022.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee — the standard first step, and as it turned out the last one.

No further action of any kind followed: no hearing, no committee vote, no amendment, no floor vote. The bill sat in committee until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, at which point it expired.

The bill carried heavy industry backing on the pro side — major film and music rights holders had long sought just this kind of mandated filtering — and equally intense opposition from internet advocacy groups and the tech industry, which warned it would mandate error-prone upload filters.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary internet users and online platforms, large and small, are better off: no filtering mandate, no new statutory-damages liability, and no government-designated surveillance technologies were imposed. The copyright industries that lobbied for it gained nothing.

for.name: Thom Tillis
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-NC), lead sponsor, member of the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where he could have pressed for a hearing or markup but none occurred.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-VT), the bill's sole cosponsor (1 of 48 Senate Democrats), former chair of the Judiciary Committee's intellectual property subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as cosponsor; the bill was introduced on his behalf alongside Tillis.

for.name: Motion Picture Association and major film studios
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported legislation to mandate copyright filtering technology on online services; industry groups had pushed similar 'technical measures' proposals for years.

for.name: Recording Industry Association of America and major music labels
for.what_they_did: Backed mandatory designation of audio-recognition filtering technology as a way to police infringement on user-generated-content platforms.

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it remained pending in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Electronic Frontier Foundation and other internet advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, warning it would force platforms to deploy error-prone upload filters that censor lawful speech and create security and privacy risks.

against.name: Tech industry trade associations (internet platforms and startups)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing government-designated filtering would burden small providers, entrench proprietary filtering technologies, and chill innovation.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — one Republican lead sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — but with only two supporters, no hearing, and no recorded vote, no partisan pattern ever emerged.

industries.industry: Movie studios, music labels, and other large copyright owners
industries.note: The bill hands them a new legal weapon: petition the government to make their preferred identification or filtering technology mandatory, then collect statutory damages from platforms that fall short. It shifts the labor and cost of enforcing their copyrights onto the platforms and, through filtering, onto users whose lawful posts get caught in the nets.

industries.industry: Online platforms and internet service providers
industries.note: Providers of services that store or transmit user content would face compliance costs, litigation risk, and statutory damages, and the smallest providers — comment sections, forums, startups — have the least capacity to implement or contest designations. Their interest in resisting tracks users' interest in an unfiltered internet.

A government designation would make a vendor's technology a required standard across an industry, and the bill allows licensing on a 'reasonable royalty' basis rather than only royalty-free — a designation converts a private product into mandatory infrastructure with a built-in revenue stream.
